claims.text: Applying a 5–10 μm Al2O3 coating to a refractory high-entropy alloy improves its high-temperature oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
The applied Al2O3 coating forms a protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer prevents oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Preventing oxygen diffusion into the alloy reduces its oxidation rate.
The coating should provide improved oxygen resistance at 1000–1200 °C in air for 100 hours.
The coated alloy will have a 50–70% lower oxidation rate than the untreated alloy.
The magnitude of the oxidation-rate reduction depends on the specific alloy composition.
The magnitude of the oxidation-rate reduction depends on the coating application method.
Coated and uncoated refractory high-entropy alloys should be compared under the same specified oxidation conditions.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if the coated alloy's oxidation rate is not at least 30% lower than that of the uncoated alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a 50–70% oxidation-rate reduction, but the stated rule only falsifies reductions below 30%. A measured reduction of 30–49% would contradict the quantitative prediction while not falsifying the hypothesis under the proposed rule.
